text: Fifteen minutes is hardly time for a party to warm up, which may be why the guests move as though the dance had begun before they arrived. Maya Deren films a social gathering — greetings, a hand taken, a head turned — as choreography, and lets figures out of Greek legend stand behind the ordinary business of being introduced to strangers. The rules of the room become the rules of a rite: repetition, exchange, one gesture answered by the same gesture. At this length nothing has to be explained, so a look can carry what a whole scene would carry elsewhere. It sits on the BBC's list of the hundred greatest films directed by women, and what surprises is how much of it plays as plain social observation: who is watched, who is handed along, what hands do when there is nothing to say.

The film Anna Silver has come to Germany to present is never itself the subject; the platforms, corridors and rented rooms between screenings are. Chantal Akerman gives her two hours and eight minutes and spends them on arrivals and departures. People find Anna easy to talk to, which is to say they talk: a man on a bench, a mother, a face from years ago, each unloading something intimate into a silence that does not close around it. She listens. She does not trade. Les Rendez-vous d'Anna is a Belgian film in French moving through German cities, so every exchange carries the faint labour of a language chosen rather than owned, and what accumulates is not the story of a woman with a career but a record of hotel geometry — bed, window, switch by the door — and of how much a person can be told and still leave in the morning.

A holiday dinner party, the kind where everyone knows the order of the evening and the talk runs on habit. John Huston stays inside eighty-three minutes and, for most of them, inside one house, letting a roomful of guests be pleasant at each other. Nothing in the manners is careless; the exactness is the method, because in company like this what a person declines to say is most of the information. The Academy Award in its record for costume design earns its keep: in a film that never leaves a gathering, cloth does the work of exposition, fixing era, income and the effort each guest has made. Afterwards a husband and wife are left with the evening behind them, and a subject neither planned to raise comes up between them. It is a small shift in temperature, and Huston takes his time over it.

The river is filthy and a shoot needs a body in the water; a young man gets in, and afterwards his neck will not come straight. From that, Tsai Ming-liang makes 116 minutes: consultations, remedies, hands laid on a body by people who mean well and cannot help. The pain carries no meaning and no dignity. It is simply there each morning, and the day arranges itself around having it looked at. Taiwan in 1997 supplies the texture: a polluted river hired as a location, a city where hours of travel end in nothing definite. Drama and Romance are the genres on file, and the second is the odder fit, since what passes for tenderness here arrives sideways, in the touch of someone paid to press on a neck. The Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize went to a film whose central event is a tilted head.

The summer holiday at his father's is over, and the boy who comes home is courteous. Kira Muratova watches what that courtesy does to a flat where mother and son have always lived on top of each other. The grievance has no incident to attach itself to — nothing said, nothing refused — so it emerges as fuss, as jokes made too loudly, as plans nobody asked for. Ninety-four minutes is long enough for a household of two to run out of subjects. Made in the Soviet Union in 1971, the film now appears on a list of the hundred best films in the history of Ukrainian cinema, which is one way of saying its address has changed while the flat has not. The teenager's silence is not cruelty. It is the beginning of leaving, conducted at the dinner table by someone too young to name it.

Money is folded inside something bought for small change at a yard sale, and the woman who sold it does not know it is gone. Sean Baker starts an unequal friendship from there: Jane is twenty-one, Sadie is old, and everything between them rests on a secret one of them keeps. The film is patient about how such an arrangement works day to day — errands, lifts, a routine invented as cover and then continued because it suits them both. Across 103 minutes neither woman is softened to make the acquaintance easier to accept, and the gap in age is never treated as charming in itself. What holds attention is the ordinary labour of company: learning somebody else's habits and hours, one of them doing it for a reason she cannot say out loud.

After closing time a Paris shopping centre becomes a dormitory, and the people hiding in it have the whole inventory to themselves. Bertrand Bonello builds the film in two unequal halves. The first is logistics: young people crossing the city on separate routes, keeping to a timetable explained to nobody outside it, their reasons left as thin as a general tiredness with the world. The second shuts them indoors with unlimited stock and a night to fill. 131 minutes, and the pressure does not come from any investigation; it comes from a group who staked everything on one afternoon and now have hours left over. A retail floor is not designed to be lived in. Bonello lets that fact do the work, watching people who wanted to end a way of life spend the night inside its display windows.

Gojo is a town in Japan small enough that a visiting film crew counts as an event, and the crew that turns up is Korean. Jang Kun-jae follows a documentary director trying to get the place on record — questions asked through the language gap, answers given by the few people who stayed — and then lets a second kind of film grow out of the same streets, one where two strangers meet who might have been invented by the first. 97 minutes, and the seam between the halves stays visible by design. Half the pleasure is recognition: a lane, a shopfront, a stretch of railway line, altered by whoever walks down it the second time. Rotterdam's audience gave it their award, which fits a film assembled out of ordinary courtesy — a question politely answered, an afternoon extended because neither party wants to end it.

The dining room is full, and that is the problem: a busy restaurant is a machine nobody can slow down once it has started. Philip Barantini keeps a head chef at the centre of it and makes him carry both halves of his life at once — the professional emergencies that arrive by the minute and the personal ones that were there before his shift began. Ninety-two minutes, a London kitchen, a brigade paid too little to absorb somebody else's bad night. The film is a workplace study before it is a thriller: hierarchy, deference, the way an order shouted at one end of a room becomes somebody's humiliation at the other. What holds the eye is not whether the service survives. It is authority running down like a battery in a man required to stay calm where the customers can see him.

The job is straightforward: kill a retired mob boss who no longer troubles anyone. Lee Hyun-seung stretches it over 122 minutes, which is a long while to keep a gun in a coat pocket, and the length is the point. Action, drama and romance sit uneasily side by side here. The old man's retirement is domestic and unhurried, full of the small competences of a person with time; the plan around him stays a piece of work with a deadline and people waiting on a result. What complicates the arrangement is not conscience so much as liking — proximity doing what proximity does. Hindsight is patient about exactly the stretch most thrillers cut: the days in which a target turns into someone with habits, and the woman watching him acquires habits of her own.

A student stands in for her sick roommate, borrows a set of interview questions, and sits down opposite a man whose office is arranged so that sitting down feels like a concession. Sam Taylor-Johnson is most alert in that register — glass, appointments, staff, a wealth that expresses itself as other people's scheduling. What follows plays less as seduction than as negotiation: terms proposed, terms queried, a good part of the 125 minutes given to what each party will consent to and in which words. Anastasia Steele is inexperienced and not for that reason naive, and she keeps asking. Its fame with a general audience arrived at once and has not really receded. Seen now, the odd thing is how procedural it all is — a romance whose central prop is a document, its charge dependent on somebody reading the terms closely.
